text: The short version is that Cassini had almost no fuel left and was being pulled out of orbit, but NASA chose to dive it into Saturn’s atmosphere so it wouldn’t drift off and later hit a moon, especially Titan or Enceladus. Those moons are interesting because they could have environments suitable for life, so keeping them clean was part of the plan. It wasn’t just a failure mode; it was a deliberate endgame, turning the last little bit of fuel into a controlled descent. For me the interesting part is that scientists were deliberately protecting possible habitats, not just saving the mission.

It's not just the pushing leg doing the work. The leg you're standing on has to support your full body weight while the other leg cycles underneath you, so that stationary leg gets a lot of load. I think what happens is your standing leg gets tense and tired from the constant pressure, and if your form is a bit off, or the deck is too low or too high, that leg takes even more strain. The muscles are working hard to keep you balanced, not just standing still.

A few things make this worse. If you're riding with your back leg bent or locked too much, the strain builds up there. Also, if you're pushing with the other leg and your standing leg is doing all the stabilizing, you're asking it to do more than it can comfortably handle. Over time that's where the pain or soreness comes from.

The fix is pretty straightforward once you know what's going on. You can switch which leg you push with more often so neither leg gets overused. Make sure your skateboard setup suits your height, because a too-low deck forces you to crouch more, adding unnecessary strain to the standing leg. And try to relax that leg a bit; a stiff locked knee doesn't help, and you can also add a small cushion or insole if it's a surface issue rather than form.

Honestly, the most practical thing is to alternate push legs and check your posture while riding. A little adjustment there usually takes the edge off the pain.

I think it’s easy to see where the confusion comes from. “Afro-American” is more commonly written as “African American” in everyday US usage, and the label points back to the African roots of the community, not necessarily to the place where the person was born or grew up.

Most Americans of African descent trace their ancestry to West and Central Africa, because that’s where the enslaved people who built much of that community came from. So the term is less about current geography and more about shared heritage. It doesn’t mean every person there was literally born on the continent. It’s a broad cultural and historical descriptor.

It’s a little awkward that the word “African” in the label can be misread. But the intent is to acknowledge that ancestry, not to make a strict passport claim.

For the Syrian state, weapons come mainly from Russia, China, Iran and Israel, though that depends on which side you mean in the civil war, so the answer isn't uniform. Nonstate actors rely on smuggling, captured gear, black-market deals and local repairs. Even after years of fighting, demand stays high because the war is still unresolved and both governments and groups want firepower to hold ground. Supply keeps moving through borders, sea routes and informal networks, so access never fully cuts off.

Honestly, I think the premise that all drugs are bad is a bit of an exaggeration, because plenty of them are pretty harmless if used as directed, like caffeine or some mild allergy meds. But the question is really about the heavy hitters that give intense euphoria, and that is where the mess starts.

When you take something like heroin or coke, it is basically hijacking the brain's reward system by dumping a massive amount of dopamine into your neurons. (Well, mostly it's a sudden chemical flood that makes the brain try to balance itself out.) To counteract that flood, the brain starts shutting down its own natural production of the chemical, which is exactly why you develop tolerance. You end up needing a bigger and bigger dose to feel the same high, and when you stop taking the drug, your baseline mood and energy are left completely depressed. That is why withdrawal feels so awful, and it's a built-in feedback loop that makes the intense pleasure come with a heavy price tag.

I think you can't have the massive dopamine spike without the brain reacting to it. A drug that gives intense euphoria with 0 adverse effects would have to trigger the reward center without making the brain adjust its own chemical balance, which is basically a contradiction in terms for how our nervous systems are wired. I am pretty sure if a drug doesn't change how the brain regulates itself, it won't give that intense, sustained high you are asking about. You would just feel normal again almost immediately.

So it's all about the neurochemistry of reward and the brain's constant need to maintain equilibrium. The intense euphoria is exactly what forces the brain to recalibrate, and that recalibration is where the adverse effects of dependence start. The drug isn't acting like a direct poison to your organs, the damage is the brain's own defensive adjustment to a chemical shock.

Hi,

I think the pain is real, and it likely comes from sustained muscle tension, not just a headache. On a long shopping day, you're walking, waiting, carrying or pushing things, holding your jaw or neck in a fixed posture, and processing crowds, lights, and noise. That combination can make the face, jaw, neck and shoulders ache in a way that feels different from a normal headache. Give yourself breaks, carry weight in a bag you hold loosely, drink water, and stop earlier when you first notice the ache. It's a warning sign, not something to push through.

Good question, and honestly this is one of those products that sounds useful until you see how much it has to compromise. A dedicated shampoo is formulated mainly for hair. A conditioner is made to soften and detangle. A bodywash is made to clean skin without being too harsh. A 3-in-1 has to cover all three jobs in one bottle, so the surfactants are usually chosen to be mild enough for skin and hair, but not as strong or as specialized as the separate versions. The conditioning part is there, but it is not the same as a real conditioner because it has to rinse away and still let the product work as a bodywash.

I think the real difference from a 2-in-1 is that the 3-in-1 tries to clean the whole body as well, so it is usually milder and more balanced. A 2-in-1 is mostly about hair, and its formulation is tuned for shampoo plus conditioning, not for scrubbing a full body wash. The tradeoff is obvious: convenience, but less targeted cleaning and less softening. I use separate products when I care about either really clean skin or really smooth hair.

I was curious about this too. GPS is the main tool here. Surveyors set up permanent ground stations with GPS receivers and compare their positions over years. That gives you how far a point on the crust has moved and at what speed. Satellites help refine the model of Earth's shape and rotation, so measurements can be tied to a common reference frame like ITRF. Because continents shift only a few centimeters a year, you need repeated observations over months or years to see the trend. GPS stations can be placed on different tectonic plates or across a mountain range, and comparing their positions over time shows the relative motion. You can also compare different stations to get the rate of separation or convergence between landmasses, which is basically how plate speeds are calculated. The numbers are small enough that you need a network of stations rather than a single receiver. I've read enough geodesy stuff to know that even GPS drifts a little, so the corrections matter. There's also seismic and geological evidence, but for a direct speed estimate, repeated GPS positions are the standard approach. I think that's the practical answer to your question. Let me know if you want the technical bits.

Cheers,
Alex

When two closely related people have a child, the child inherits genes from both parents. Because they share ancestors, they are much more likely to carry the same rare recessive mutations. Normally, a single copy of a harmful gene is masked by the other normal copy, but if both parents pass down the same mutation, the child ends up with two copies and the effect becomes visible. Some of these mutations touch genes involved in brain development and cognitive function, so the child's IQ can come out lower than average. It's not that inbreeding directly lowers intelligence; it's that the child has a higher chance of expressing harmful recessive traits, including some that affect cognition. There isn't one single gene; it's the accumulated genetic load from multiple small effects. In practice, the effect is probabilistic, not guaranteed for every child.

Honestly, I think the main reason is that most people can protect their arms when they get hit, and the arm is also good at taking impact without the whole body having to compensate. If you get hit in the arm, you can tense it, pull it in, or brace with your hand. That local response can keep the shock from spreading through the whole body, and it can make the pain seem more contained. Well, mostly. Other parts of the body, like your head or torso, are much harder to guard or protect quickly. So the difference isn’t that the arm feels less sensitive, it’s that the arm is easier to defend, and the body can keep the effect in one spot. I think that’s the practical difference.

Carbon monoxide is dangerous because it interferes with the oxygen-carrying system in your blood, not because the gas itself is chemically corrosive. When you breathe in CO, it latches onto hemoglobin in red blood cells with a strength roughly 200 times that of oxygen. Hemoglobin is the protein responsible for transporting oxygen to every tissue in the body. Once CO takes those binding sites, oxygen can’t get carried where it’s needed. This doesn’t just mean there’s less oxygen available; it also makes the oxygen that is bound release less readily to tissues. The result is a kind of internal suffocation: organs keep demanding oxygen, but the delivery system has been jammed. That is why carbon monoxide is so poisonous to breathe.

Carbon dioxide is a different story. It’s the waste gas your cells produce after using oxygen, and your lungs and breathing rate normally keep it in check. At everyday levels it isn’t a problem, and the body treats rising CO2 as a signal to breathe deeper. That’s why you don’t usually notice it in ordinary life. High levels can still make you dizzy, sleepy, or short of breath, so it isn’t harmless at all, but its main danger comes from changing the acidity of your blood and stressing breathing, rather than binding tightly to the oxygen carrier.

So the core difference is mechanism. CO poisons by occupying the oxygen transport system itself. CO2 mainly affects you through the breathing and acid-base balance. That distinction is why carbon monoxide feels so sneaky: you can be exposed without obvious immediate pain, while your tissues quietly starve. For a wiki, the practical takeaway is that CO’s threat is its strong binding to hemoglobin, while CO2 at normal levels is just normal body chemistry doing its job.

In an aircraft emergency, the brace position is not about being still; it is about controlling the body when the plane hits the ground. When an aircraft stops very quickly, our bodies keep moving because of inertia. The brace asks you to bring your body into a compact, supported shape so that less energy has to be absorbed by internal organs and soft tissues. You lean forward, keep your head close to the aircraft surface behind you, and use your hands to support your weight. This helps keep the head from striking a seatback or floor, limits the distance the torso can move, and reduces the risk of neck, spine, or abdominal injury. It also keeps the airway more open and makes it easier for you to get up and evacuate after impact. If you are not strapped in, use the brace as a way to stabilize yourself while you fasten the belt and shoulder harness. Most people remember it as hands on legs, feet flat, head protected, body low. In short, bracing turns a large, uncontrolled movement into a smaller, controlled one, which is exactly what the body needs during a hard landing.

Most businesses before the industrial era were small, local, and often family-run, so they rarely left the kind of widespread records we use to define "well known." Even when they were successful, they usually served one town or trade network, and their names faded when owners changed or the business was absorbed. A few earlier guilds or trading houses existed, but they weren't household names in the way modern brands are.

The industrial era changed this because factories, railways, and mass markets made companies much larger and easier to recognize. That is why the names people remember are mostly from that later period, not from the centuries before it.

I think the dealership's lower rate is a bit of a trap. The bank wins on total cost most of the time, and I'm pretty sure you should always compare the actual monthly payment and total interest over the whole loan, not just the headline rate.

A dealer can advertise a low percentage, but they often stretch the loan out longer than you need, or add charges that quietly kill the savings. I remember seeing a quote where the dealership rate was 2% lower than my bank, but the loan was 72 months instead of 48. That extra time means paying interest on interest for a long stretch. The bank might quote a higher rate, but a shorter loan means less total interest. That's the angle I'd focus on.

There's also the fee side. Dealerships sometimes bake in documentation fees, add-on products, or higher principal through "value added products." If the loan amount is bigger at the dealer, the lower rate matters less. The bank usually keeps it simple: you borrow the actual price and pay a flat monthly amount.

Honestly, the rate alone doesn't tell the story. I've seen this enough to trust the rule: total interest paid and total loan term decide the winner. If the dealer's lower rate comes with a 60 month loan and the bank's higher rate comes with a 36 month loan, the bank can still be cheaper overall.

One more thing, and this is where people get burned: the dealer's advertised rate often only applies to qualified customers or limited inventory. You can end up paying the higher "regular" rate. The bank's rate might be the same for everyone, which makes it easier to plan around.

I'd always run both numbers side by side. Same car, same loan term, then compare total cost. If the dealer's rate is lower but the term is longer, that's usually the tell. The cheaper-looking rate isn't the cheaper loan. That's the position I'm taking.

I’m in favor of making marijuana legal everywhere in the US, but mostly at the state level, because that’s already how it works. Right now, you can walk into a dispensary in California or Colorado, while in some states a tiny amount is still a crime. That patchwork is messy, but it lets places adjust their own rules. What bothers me is the inconsistency. One state can tax and regulate sales, while a neighboring state might still treat possession as a misdemeanor. I don’t think the federal government should override that. States should decide, but when they do, they should stop pretending use is always a small offense.

I think the key is that electricity in the body is really just ions moving across cell membranes, not some magical spark. Nerve cells keep a charge difference, and when those gates open, sodium and potassium rush in or out. That’s the signal.

It’s not dramatic at all. It’s slow, chemical, and mostly quiet. I’m pretty sure it feels like electricity because it moves fast enough to make you twitch or think, but underneath it’s just cells balancing charges. Honestly, that’s the whole trick.

I think most people get sampling backwards. They hear a chopped 45 second fragment in a hit song and assume someone just dug into a crate of vinyl and cut one line out. But in my experience, the interesting part is the clearance work that happens before a single note gets placed.

You start with a track you want to build around, but the snippet has to match the BPM you're working in. So if the original is slower, you either slow down your beat or stretch the sample. Time-stretching is fiddly; you're trading fidelity for pitch, and it can make the vocal sound muddy. Some producers instead cut the fragment, nudge the tempo per section, and edit it to fit.

Then there's rights. If you're using a piece of an older record, you need permission from the master's owner, the label, and often the writer and performer. A single bar of a song can trigger all of those negotiations. I'm pretty sure that's the piece most beginners miss. It's not about finding the best melody line, it's about whether anyone will let you use it.

Once it's cleared, the actual musical work begins. You'll layer the sample under a new kit, maybe run it through a compressor and a bit of distortion, and let it sit behind the new bassline. The old recording should feel like a texture, not a copy. If it fights the rest of the track, you'll either swap the sample or re-arrange the song around it. Honestly, the most satisfying tracks are the ones where the sample barely stands out, but you still know which record it came from.

The practical detail I keep coming back to is the edit. A raw snippet is useless until it's trimmed, pitch-shifted, and time-aligned with the new arrangement. That's where the craft is.

I can’t even tell you if the food is good because we never got to eat. We arrived at 7:20 p.m. on Sunday, picking this place specifically because we had a 10:00 p.m. show in the same hotel and figured it’d be easy. We put our names into their completely useless digital waitlist and were told to come back to pay at 8:23 p.m. We did, but then stood around until 8:40 p.m. before staff casually mentioned we probably wouldn’t be seated until 9:15. It was only a party of two, and they offered zero solutions. If the wait extends that far past payment, tell people upfront so our night isn’t completely wasted. Total disaster. Zero stars if that were an option.

I went to this buffet on a Friday around 4:30 p.m., and surprisingly there was no line at all. The two of us paid about $130, which felt pretty steep. Before going I had figured the price would be comparable to a steakhouse, but afterward I learned the buffet actually cost somewhat more than I had expected to pay at one.

Honestly, I was disappointed that steak wasn’t offered. At that price I assumed there would be some kind of steak option. The meat choices included lamb, prime rib, and chicken, but those are things I feel like you can find at other Las Vegas buffets for much less money. The seafood station had Alaskan crab legs and rock crab claws. Alaskan crab legs show up at a lot of Vegas buffets, but I hadn’t run into rock crab claws anywhere else, so those were interesting. The problem was there were no crab-claw crackers. Staff said wooden mallets were available, but our table was so close to the next table that I didn’t want to start smashing crab shells and send pieces flying at the people next to us, so I just ate the crab legs.

The Asian station didn’t seem especially distinctive either. It reminded me quite a bit of the buffet at Rampart Casino. Dessert had gelato and various pastries, but nothing really stood out. They also had fresh juices, although I didn’t try any. Overall, I’d call the buffet acceptable, but overpriced for what it offers. If you’re curious, it’s worth trying once, especially if there’s no wait. But if the line is long, I’d probably reconsider.
